head: A Japanese taste for Tasmanian soba put 300 cherry trees along a Tasmanian river.
summary: Buckwheat trials began in Tasmania in 1986, and its reversed seasons let Japanese millers buy fresh soba flour twice a year. Mill owner Rick Shiratori donated the cherry trees thirty years ago in thanks, and 300 now line the Meander River at Deloraine, blooming for about ten days. Around 200 people came on Sunday to the fifth Hanami Trail festival for aikido, taiko drumming and bamboo flute.

head: Gibbons got Marmite-smeared poles and gift-wrapped locusts for their zoo's fiftieth birthday.
summary: Orana Wildlife Park in Christchurch marked fifty years since it opened on 25 September 1976 with birthday enrichment for its animals. The gibbons had Marmite and peanut butter smeared on poles, plus gift-wrapped boxes of cooked corn and live locusts to unwrap. The party came days after ratepayers gave the park a NZ$1.2 million lifeline.

head: Oxford's dictionary made room for Bermudian and Caribbean slang.
summary: The Oxford English Dictionary added more than a dozen words long used across Bermuda and the Caribbean, including bimpert, a Bermudian term for a foolish person, and canboulay, Trinidad's 1800s emancipation-carnival tradition. Lexicographers drew on decades of everyday use, from hamma, Bermudian for friend, to vex money, the Caribbean term for a woman's emergency cash reserve. The update gives formal recognition to language islanders have spoken for generations, alongside dishes like peanut punch and sugar cake.

head: Volunteers turned a windswept Scottish train platform into an award-winning garden.
summary: The Royal Horticultural Society gave its first-ever Railway Stations in Bloom prize to Cardross station on Scotland's west coast, chosen from five shortlisted stations across Britain. Since 2022, the Cardross Community Organic Garden group led by Jane Connolly has planted every available bed with fruit trees and vegetables, turning a once-bare stop into somewhere people travel to see. Judges praised how the group pulled in schoolchildren, Brownies, and other volunteers along the way.

head: A youth committee brought lantern-making and dough-figurine carving back to Penang's Mid-Autumn Festival.
summary: On the Esplanade in George Town, organizers revived a full slate of Mid-Autumn customs this week, from lantern-riddle games to mooncake-making demonstrations. The Clan-Associations Youth Committee's Goh Kok Liang added dough-figurine carving, paper-cutting, and Sichuan opera face-changing to old standbys like hopscotch and the wind-fire wheel, drawing families ahead of the festival's September 25 date. The point, he said, is giving young people in a modern port city an easy, everyday way to hold onto a shared tradition.

head: A ban on compressor diving revived an ancestral freediving skill in Indonesia.
summary: In the Bajau fishing village of Poto Tano, octopus hunters once dropped to the seafloor trailing air hoses from a compressor; a 2020 ban made the older skill of freediving 15 to 20 meters with a handmade lure called a pocong valuable again. Only about ten people in the community can still use the pocong well, and the roughly 40 fishers of the PELITA brotherhood now close two or three fishing grounds at a time, for months, so the octopus can recover. They find their way by reading stars, wind, and current rather than GPS, a practice a local women's conservation group is now helping document and pass on to the next generation.

head: A Burgundy village reopened its only cafe-bistro after eight months dark.
summary: When Au Bon Accueil in Saint-Martin-sur-Ouanne closed for eight months, the village had already lost its bakery eight years earlier, so village mayor Hervé Chapuis and the wider Charny-Orée-de-Puisaye council put in €25,000 to renovate it. New manager Nadia Letellier reopened the doors this month, saying, "It's so important to have a cafe-bistro in a village like this. We couldn't let it stay closed." Aurélien Pécot, who ran a bistro himself for seven years before becoming the area's mayor, says regulars need their "point of reference" — one reason the council now owns five such properties across its 14 villages, in a country that has lost all but 40,000 of the 500,000 cafe-bistros it had a century ago.

head: Nearly 1,200 Star Trek fans raised their hands together for a world record.
summary: At London's Science Museum on September 10, 1,188 fans performed the split-fingered Vulcan salute to mark the franchise's 60th anniversary. Guinness World Records adjudicator Paulina Sapinska counted 934 people holding the gesture for a full minute, enough for a new record in a category that had never existed before, with actor Martin Quinn joining the crowd. Sapinska called it "a huge bonding moment," proof a fictional hand sign can still pull a room of strangers together.

head: Archaeologists opened a Chimú tomb that had stayed sealed for six hundred years.
summary: Archaeologists at Chan Chan, Peru, unsealed an intact Chimú mausoleum holding the remains of at least 38 people, buried roughly six centuries ago with metal weapons, gold and copper ornaments, and fine textiles. Lead archaeologist Jorge Meneses said it was the first time researchers have found an elite Chimú burial platform with its contents undisturbed, in a complex where only 7 percent has been excavated. Anthropologist Gabriel Prieto called it "the discovery of the decade."

head: A metal detectorist dug up two Viking silver hoards in one afternoon.
summary: Kalle Lappinen was searching a field in his hometown of Sysmä, Finland, when his detector signaled sharply, leading him to a hoard of compacted 11th-century coins about eighteen inches down, then a second nearby hoard with more coins, a silver bead, a bracelet and a charm. The roughly ten pounds of silver mark the largest Viking-era find in Finnish history, and archaeologist Eljas Oksanen praised Lappinen's decision to report it right away as "responsible and responsive detecting." The silver is now being studied and preserved at Lahti City Museums, adding fresh evidence of Viking-age trade reaching deep into Finland.
